name: Claude Code, on your own machine
operator: Anthropic (the vendor); each user is the operator of their own deployment
basis: the vendor’s own documentation and a published deployment shape
what: The command-line coding agent, running as the user’s own account on their machine, with the settings it ships with.
note: An example scan of a product as its vendor documents it, not of any one deployment. Disclosure: the agent that wrote this scan runs on this product.

grant.product: Claude Code (the CLI, on your own machine)
grant.statement: This describes a published deployment shape. It is not an assessment, an audit, a certification or a security review of any named product, and it carries no adjective and no score.

I04.n: The vendor calls it "an agentic coding tool that reads your codebase, edits files, runs commands".

I08.n: It edits files, runs commands, stages changes, commits and opens pull requests.

I10.n: The codebase, the shell, git and the development tools it integrates with.

I11.n: It can connect to Model Context Protocol servers; a project’s servers have their own approval prompt.

I16.n: In Manual mode shell commands and edits ask before they run; file reads in the working directory do not.

I18.n: In auto mode a classifier reviews actions instead of prompting; an action it blocks is listed, and the person can approve it so Claude may retry.
I18.span: approve the action so Claude may retry

I20.n: The vendor states what the product is for.

I21.n: Allow, ask and deny rules per tool and pattern.

I22.n: The security page states limits, for example that an approved shell command can write anywhere the account can.

I23.n: A published deployment shape lists 16 capabilities from 22 tool rows; it says none of the rows is measured and all 22 are derived.

I38.n: Shell commands (beyond a read-only set) and edits need approval in Manual mode.

I39.n: Esc stops the current response or tool call mid-turn, and Ctrl+C interrupts a running operation.
I39.span: Stop the current response or tool call mid-turn so you can redirect

I41.n: Tool activity can be exported as OpenTelemetry events; it is configured by the operator.

I43.n: Usage, cost and tool activity across an organisation, through OpenTelemetry.

I46.n: "The boundary is a permission prompt, so a Bash command you approve can still write anywhere your user account can."
I46.span: a Bash command you approve can still write anywhere your user account can

I48.n: An organisation can deliver managed settings that a user’s own files do not change; hooks run on every tool call and can block it. This is an enforcement mechanism, not a policy.

I61.n: The model configuration page lists the models it uses by alias (Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, Fable) and the version each alias resolves to for each provider.
I61.span: Uses the latest Opus model for complex reasoning tasks

I63.n: The vendor points to a SOC 2 Type 2 report and an ISO 27001 certificate at its trust centre; they cover the vendor, not a user’s deployment.

I12.n: Agent teams coordinate several instances, each in its own context, that message each other. The vendor says they "are experimental and disabled by default".

S1.n: A vendor case study names a customer and a figure: Stripe deployed it to 1,370 engineers.
S1.span: Deployed Claude Code to 1,370 engineers with a zero-configuration setup

S2.n: The vendor’s community marketplace holds third-party plugins their authors submitted, and the page says many plugins sit in their authors’ own marketplaces.
S2.span: Third-party plugins that their authors submitted to Anthropic

S3.n: The documentation publishes an llms.txt index.

I56.n: By default it adds a Co-Authored-By trailer naming the Claude model to its commits and a Generated with Claude Code line to pull request descriptions; a setting can change or hide both.
I56.span: The name is the model in use when the commit is made

I58.n: A page describes what data is sent, kept and used.

I57.n: A feedback command and a bug command send reports to the vendor.

I45.n: Sandboxing restricts shell commands at the operating system level (filesystem and network); the operator turns it on.

configurations.name: As shipped
configurations.note: Manual mode: shell commands and edits ask first.

configurations.name: Sandbox on
configurations.note: Shell commands confined by the operating system.

configurations.name: Auto mode
configurations.note: A classifier reviews actions instead of the person.

configurations.name: Managed by an organisation
configurations.note: Managed settings, permission rules and telemetry.

configurations.name: Auto mode, tools and agent teams
configurations.note: Everything that widens what it does.

moved: As above. Managed settings are recorded as an enforcement mechanism, not as a policy in force.

findings.finding: The quoted span "Stripe rolled out Claude Code to 1,370 engineers." is not in the source. The page (read 2026-11-10) says "Deployed Claude Code to 1,370 engineers with a zero-configuration setup". The fact and the figure are right; the span is a paraphrase presented as a quotation. Quote the page exactly, under fifteen words, or drop the span.

"The product and its model family are named" is not what the indicator asks (the models and third-party components it uses are listed). I searched the overview page and found no model named. Either cite a page that lists the models (the model configuration page), or remove the answer.

The note says most rows are "derived, not measured". The profile itself says all 22 of its rows are derived and none measured ("every row is a claim until somebody runs the probes"). Say none are measured. Grade documented is right for the profile as a document; the scope for I23 says a grant profile only, which the source is.

The source cited (permissions) supports "a deny rule removes a tool" and the person can decline a prompt. Neither is a way to pause or stop the agent. I did not find an interrupt or stop statement on that page. Cite a page that says the person can interrupt a running session, or lower the credit.

Credited as available (auto mode). The source says in auto mode "a classifier reviews actions instead of you". The indicator is that the person approves critical decisions only; a classifier standing in for the person is a different fact. Round two will argue whether this credit holds.

The page tells an author how to publish a marketplace and says "anyone with access registers it". That shows the mechanism, not that any third party has published one. The scope asks for third parties publishing. Cite a page that names third-party plugins or marketplaces, or lower the credit.

The span "Claude Code is an AI-powered coding assistant" is in the source and under fifteen words. But it is the documentation describing the product to a reader, not the agent telling the people it talks to that it is an AI. Weak credit for this indicator; consider whether it should stand.

Grade documented, mode available, source the sandbox page. The scope says this indicator is read from a measured grant only, and the grant is derived. The answer is accurate; the credit should come from the grant, not from the page. Check how the scorer treats it.

Opened each source. The note says what the source says; grade documented is right for each (S3 observed: llms.txt fetched, resolves); mode is right (I11, I12, I18, I21, I41, I43, I45, I48 are available and tied to a configuration; the rest are the default). Spans in I46 (13 words) and I56 (7) are in the source. Quoted text in I04 (12 words) and I12 is in the source. I63 credit is limited, as the note says, to the vendor.
The "max" configuration is "Auto mode, tools and agent teams": the three flags it turns on exist (auto, mcp, teams) and each is documented. No finding.

review.note: Published as an example on 10 November 2026, before the review workflow existed. Mapped by one agent. It goes through two rounds of review next.

responses.response: Span replaced with the page’s own words, verified on the page read 2026-11-10: "Deployed Claude Code to 1,370 engineers with a zero-configuration setup" (10 words). Fact and figure unchanged.
Source moved to the model configuration page, which lists the models by alias and the version each resolves to per provider; span verified there. The overview names no model, as the reviewer found.

Note corrected: the profile counts 22 tool rows, none measured and all 22 derived, behind 16 capabilities. Grade and source unchanged; as an operation fact it does not count toward a level held, which products do not get anyway.

Source moved to the interactive mode page, which says Esc stops the current response or tool call mid-turn and Ctrl+C interrupts a running operation; span verified. The permissions page did not support a stop.

Kept, re-sourced to the permission modes page: in auto mode an action the classifier blocks is listed and the person can approve it so Claude may retry, which is the person approving the critical step only. Note: that page also says auto is the built-in default in a terminal from v2.1.283, which round two should weigh against the scan’s Manual-mode "As shipped" configuration.

Source moved to the vendor’s marketplaces page, which says the community marketplace holds third-party plugins submitted by their authors and that many plugins are in their authors’ own marketplaces; span verified. That marketplace’s published catalogue (anthropics/claude-plugins-community, fetched 2026-11-10) lists third-party entries such as 0x and 42crunch-api-security-testing.

Re-sourced from the documentation’s description of itself to the settings reference: by default commits carry a Co-Authored-By trailer naming the Claude model and pull requests a Generated with Claude Code line, so reviewers of its work are told it is an AI. Read under aiact.art-50, which also covers marking AI output; round two may still judge it.

No change for this note; see the I18 response on which mode a terminal session starts in.
